```{python}
fi_line = "Häijy on kaunis ja kaunis on häijy"
el_line = "Είν' τα ωραία φρίκη, φρίκη τα καλά"
en_line = "Fair is foul, and foul is fair"

def analyze_line(line, nlp):
    doc = nlp(line)
    results = []
    for token in doc:
        results.append({
            "text": token.text,
            "lemma": token.lemma_,
            "POS": token.pos_,
            "morphology": str(token.morph)
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(results)

display(analyze_line(en_line, nlp_en))
display(analyze_line(fi_line, nlp_fi))
display(analyze_line(el_line, nlp_el))
```
Code review:
This first defines the line "fair is foul, and foul is fair" or its equivalent in each language. Then creates a new function by defining analyze lines with the inputs of which which line to analyze and which nlp to pull from. Then creates doc which finds the nlp gramatical properties for the languges and words in each line. Then you create a list called results which holds the info for the rest of the df. Then it creates a for loop that looks through each token in doc. And on each new token it .appends/adds the word, lemma, part of speech, and the morphology of each word. Then it returns a dataframe of the whats in results. Then I used an llm to figure out how to actually the data frames for each because I was using print but it said the display is what actually will show the data frame when rendered. I also had it double check my code to make sure I wasn't overlooking something.
Section reflection:
Each language uses a vastly diffrent make up of the parts of speech it uses to create the phrase fair is foul and foul is fair. I find it fasinating how translations are created and negotiated to have equivalent meanings but because context must be factored in the entire process is made more nuanced. The first mistake I can see is that it labels the second foul as an adjective which in this context it should be a noun. 
```{python}
parts = wn.synset("body_part.n.01")

def lang_body_part(df, lang):
    nouns = df[df["pos"] == "NOUN"]["lemma"].unique().dropna()
    body_parts = []
    for word in nouns:
        if is_a(word, parts, lang):
            body_parts.append(word)
    return sorted(body_parts)

print("English:", lang_body_part(en_df, "eng"))
print("Finnish:", lang_body_part(fi_df, "fin"))
print("Greek:", lang_body_part(el_df, "ell"))

for synset in wn.synsets("ball", pos=wn.NOUN):
    print(synset.name(), "→", synset.definition())
```
Code review:
First you create parts as the synset for body parts has all of the definitions for body parts in multiple languages. Now create a function that defines lang_body_parts with the inputs being the data frame you're searching and the language you are looking in. Then you makes nouns mean to check the dataframe's rows for words that are classified by nouns and then take their lemma and used .unique to only use each word once. And then I also used an llm to check my code after to make sure nothing is overlooked and it suggested .dropna which removes all missing values. Then create an empty list called body_parts to hold the rest of the functions aspects. Then you create a for loop to search for word in nouns and when you find what applys then you apply is_a function with the catagory parts from before. Then .append/add that word to the body_parts list. And then the function returns the bosy parts list sorted alphebetically. Then apply and print the function for each language dataframe. And then to check the definition of ball you create a for loop which checks synset for the term ball as a noun and then print all the synset names and all the definitions.
